name: mv
plain: `mv` moves a file or folder to a new place, or renames it. There is no separate rename command: renaming is moving to a new name in the same folder.
On the same disk a move is instant; across disks it copies then deletes.
when: Rename and keep a backup of a file you overwrite.

examples.title: Move into a folder
examples.explain: The file keeps its name and lands in the folder.

examples.title: Move several files
examples.explain: The last argument must be a folder when you give several sources.

examples.title: Ask before overwrite
examples.explain: -i asks if final.txt exists. -n skips instead of overwriting.

examples.title: Move with a backup
examples.explain: -b renames the existing target to app.conf~ first.

examples.title: Move everything from a pipeline
examples.explain: -t puts the target first so find can append many files at the end.

options.plain: Move only when the source is newer or the target is missing.
Treat the target as a normal file.

mistakes: Overwriting an existing file silently: use -i.
Moving a file onto a name that is a directory: it goes inside.
Using mv to a path that does not exist and creating a file named like a folder.
Expecting a move across disks to be atomic.
try: Rename a file, then undo it.
Move three files into a folder in one command.
Use -b and look at the backup it makes.
see_also: cp(1), rm(1), rename(1), ln(1), find(1), mkdir(1).
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
